claim: Canine transmissible venereal tumour (CTVT) is a clonally transmissible cancer that originated approximately 11,000 years ago.
source: Canine transmissible venereal tumour (CTVT) is a clonally transmissible cancer that originated approximately 11,000 years ago and affects dogs worldwide.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work establishing CTVT origin timing

claim: CTVT affects dogs worldwide.
source: Canine transmissible venereal tumour (CTVT) is a clonally transmissible cancer that originated approximately 11,000 years ago and affects dogs worldwide.
evidence: Supported by the global sample collection from 39 countries across six continents

claim: CTVT mitochondrial genomes (mtDNAs) have been acquired by periodic capture from transient hosts.
source: Despite the clonal origin of the CTVT nuclear genome, CTVT mitochondrial genomes (mtDNAs) have been acquired by periodic capture from transient hosts.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis showing five distinct CTVT mtDNA clades and previous citations

claim: 449 complete mtDNAs from a global population of CTVTs were sequenced.
source: We sequenced 449 complete mtDNAs from a global population of CTVTs, and show that mtDNA horizontal transfer has occurred at least five times, delineating five tumour clades whose distributions track two millennia of dog global migration.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and methods

claim: mtDNA horizontal transfer has occurred at least five times in CTVT.
source: We sequenced 449 complete mtDNAs from a global population of CTVTs, and show that mtDNA horizontal transfer has occurred at least five times, delineating five tumour clades whose distributions track two millennia of dog global migration.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis showing five distinct CTVT mtDNA clades

claim: Five CTVT tumour clades track two millennia of dog global migration.
source: We sequenced 449 complete mtDNAs from a global population of CTVTs, and show that mtDNA horizontal transfer has occurred at least five times, delineating five tumour clades whose distributions track two millennia of dog global migration.
evidence: Supported by geographic distribution analysis and timing estimates of clade origins

claim: Negative selection has operated to prevent accumulation of deleterious mutations in captured mtDNA.
source: Negative selection has operated to prevent accumulation of deleterious mutations in captured mtDNA, and recombination has caused occasional mtDNA re-assortment.
evidence: Supported by dN/dS analysis and VAF analysis showing reduced frequency of truncating mutations

claim: Recombination has caused occasional mtDNA re-assortment in CTVT.
source: Negative selection has operated to prevent accumulation of deleterious mutations in captured mtDNA, and recombination has caused occasional mtDNA re-assortment.
evidence: Supported by recombination detection algorithms and long-read sequencing data

claim: Functional mtDNA is a driver of CTVT global metastatic spread.
source: These findings implicate functional mtDNA as a driver of CTVT global metastatic spread, further highlighting the important role of mtDNA in cancer evolution.
evidence: Inferred from evidence of negative selection and multiple horizontal transfer events

claim: CTVT is a transmissible cancer that is contagious between dogs via the transfer of living cancer cells during coitus.
source: The canine transmissible venereal tumour (CTVT) is a transmissible cancer that is contagious between dogs via the transfer of living cancer cells during coitus.
evidence: Established knowledge about CTVT transmission

claim: CTVT usually manifests as localised tumours involving the genital mucosa in both male and female domestic dogs.
source: The disease usually manifests as localised tumours involving the genital mucosa in both male and female domestic dogs.
evidence: Established clinical knowledge about CTVT presentation

claim: CTVT first arose from the somatic cells of an individual dog that lived approximately 11,000 years ago.
source: CTVT first arose from the somatic cells of an individual dog that lived approximately 11,000 years ago; it subsequently survived beyond the death of this original animal by metastasising to new hosts (Murgia et al., 2006; Rebbeck et al., 2009; Murchison et al., 2014; Decker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: CTVT survived beyond the death of its original host animal by metastasising to new hosts.
source: CTVT first arose from the somatic cells of an individual dog that lived approximately 11,000 years ago; it subsequently survived beyond the death of this original animal by metastasising to new hosts (Murgia et al., 2006; Rebbeck et al., 2009; Murchison et al., 2014; Decker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: CTVT is found in dog populations worldwide.
source: CTVT is found in dog populations worldwide, and is the oldest and most prolific cancer lineage known in nature (Murchison et al., 2014; Strakova and Murchison, 2014; Strakova and Murchison, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations and global sample collection

claim: CTVT is the oldest and most prolific cancer lineage known in nature.
source: CTVT is found in dog populations worldwide, and is the oldest and most prolific cancer lineage known in nature (Murchison et al., 2014; Strakova and Murchison, 2014; Strakova and Murchison, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: 449 CTVT tumours and 338 matched hosts were collected from 39 countries across six continents.
source: we performed low-coverage whole genome sequencing (~0.3X whole genome coverage) on 449 CTVT tumours and 338 matched hosts collected from 39 countries across six continents (Materials and methods) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated in methods

claim: Low-coverage whole genome sequencing was performed at ~0.3X whole genome coverage.
source: we performed low-coverage whole genome sequencing (~0.3X whole genome coverage) on 449 CTVT tumours and 338 matched hosts collected from 39 countries across six continents (Materials and methods) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated in methods

claim: MtDNA was sequenced at ~70X coverage.
source: MtDNA was sequenced at ~70X coverage, indicating that each CTVT cell carries approximately 470 mtDNA copies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2, Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated in results

claim: Each CTVT cell carries approximately 470 mtDNA copies.
source: MtDNA was sequenced at ~70X coverage, indicating that each CTVT cell carries approximately 470 mtDNA copies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2, Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculated from sequencing coverage data

claim: CTVT was confirmed by identification of a characteristic rearrangement involving a long interspersed nuclear element (LINE) near the MYC locus.
source: CTVT was confirmed by identification of a characteristic rearrangement involving a long interspersed nuclear element (LINE) near the MYC locus (Katzir et al., 1985; 1987) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by qPCR assays and citations

claim: 1005 single point substitution variants were identified in the CTVT mtDNA population.
source: We identified 1005 single point substitution variants and 27 short insertions and deletions (indels) in the CTVT mtDNA population (Supplementary files 4, 5, 6, 7, 12, 13).
evidence: Directly stated in results

claim: 27 short insertions and deletions (indels) were identified in the CTVT mtDNA population.
source: We identified 1005 single point substitution variants and 27 short insertions and deletions (indels) in the CTVT mtDNA population (Supplementary files 4, 5, 6, 7, 12, 13).
evidence: Directly stated in results

claim: CTVT mtDNA somatic substitution mutations are dominated by C>T and T>C mutations showing a striking strand bias.
source: CTVT mtDNA somatic substitution mutations (see Materials and methods) had the characteristic profile that is observed in human cancers, dominated by C>T and T>C mutations showing a striking strand bias (Ju et al., 2014) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by mutational spectrum analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The CTVT mtDNA mutational process is probably replication-coupled.
source: This mutational process is probably replication-coupled, and mutations associated with this process appear to accumulate at a roughly constant rate in human cancers (Ju et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from mutational pattern and cited human cancer studies

claim: CTVT mtDNAs cluster in five distinct groups within dog mtDNA haplogroup A1.
source: A maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree constructed with mtDNA sequences from CTVT, matched hosts and 252 additional dogs (see Supplementary file 8) revealed that CTVT mtDNAs cluster in five distinct groups within dog mtDNA haplogroup A1 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: The most recent common ancestor of samples 24T (CTVT clade 1) and 79T (CTVT clade 2) existed approximately 460 years ago.
source: Although CTVT originated about 11,000 years ago, whole genome sequences of two CTVT tumours derived from clades 1 and 2 indicated that these two clades shared a common ancestor approximately 460 years ago (Murchison et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous whole genome sequencing study

claim: Clade 1 mtDNA carry more than double the number of mtDNA somatic mutations (22.5 mutations average) compared with clade 2 mtDNA (9.4 mutations average).
source: This analysis revealed that clade 1 mtDNA carry more than double the number of mtDNA somatic mutations (22.5 mutations average) compared with clade 2 mtDNA (9.4 mutations average).
evidence: Calculated from somatic mutation counts shown in Figure 1B

claim: The clade 2 mtDNA horizontal transfer event occurred no more than 460 years ago.
source: By inferring that the clade 2 mtDNA horizontal transfer event occurred no more than 460 years ago, this analysis suggests a maximum time since mtDNA uptake of 1097 years for clade 1, 244 years for clade 3, 1690 years for clade 4 and 585 years for clade 5, assuming a constant somatic accumulation of mutations in CTVT mtDNA (Materials and methods).
evidence: Inferred from nuclear genome dating and mutation rate calculations

claim: The maximum time since mtDNA uptake is 1097 years for clade 1.
source: By inferring that the clade 2 mtDNA horizontal transfer event occurred no more than 460 years ago, this analysis suggests a maximum time since mtDNA uptake of 1097 years for clade 1, 244 years for clade 3, 1690 years for clade 4 and 585 years for clade 5, assuming a constant somatic accumulation of mutations in CTVT mtDNA (Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculated from mutation accumulation rates

claim: The maximum time since mtDNA uptake is 244 years for clade 3.
source: By inferring that the clade 2 mtDNA horizontal transfer event occurred no more than 460 years ago, this analysis suggests a maximum time since mtDNA uptake of 1097 years for clade 1, 244 years for clade 3, 1690 years for clade 4 and 585 years for clade 5, assuming a constant somatic accumulation of mutations in CTVT mtDNA (Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculated from mutation accumulation rates

claim: The maximum time since mtDNA uptake is 1690 years for clade 4.
source: By inferring that the clade 2 mtDNA horizontal transfer event occurred no more than 460 years ago, this analysis suggests a maximum time since mtDNA uptake of 1097 years for clade 1, 244 years for clade 3, 1690 years for clade 4 and 585 years for clade 5, assuming a constant somatic accumulation of mutations in CTVT mtDNA (Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculated from mutation accumulation rates

claim: The maximum time since mtDNA uptake is 585 years for clade 5.
source: By inferring that the clade 2 mtDNA horizontal transfer event occurred no more than 460 years ago, this analysis suggests a maximum time since mtDNA uptake of 1097 years for clade 1, 244 years for clade 3, 1690 years for clade 4 and 585 years for clade 5, assuming a constant somatic accumulation of mutations in CTVT mtDNA (Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculated from mutation accumulation rates

claim: The original mtDNA that was present in the founder dog that first spawned CTVT is not detectable in tumours that were analysed.
source: Thus, this analysis suggests that the original mtDNA, that was present in the founder dog that first spawned CTVT, is not detectable in tumours that we have analysed, and indicates that CTVT cells have captured mtDNA from transient hosts at least five times within the last two thousand years.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis showing all CTVT mtDNAs cluster in five groups with recent origins

claim: CTVT cells have captured mtDNA from transient hosts at least five times within the last two thousand years.
source: Thus, this analysis suggests that the original mtDNA, that was present in the founder dog that first spawned CTVT, is not detectable in tumours that we have analysed, and indicates that CTVT cells have captured mtDNA from transient hosts at least five times within the last two thousand years.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and timing estimates

claim: Clades 1 and 2 occur most frequently in the CTVT population that was analysed.
source: Clades 1 and 2, which occur most frequently in the CTVT population that we analysed, both have a global distribution.
evidence: Observed from sample distribution data

claim: Clades 1 and 2 both have a global distribution.
source: Clades 1 and 2, which occur most frequently in the CTVT population that we analysed, both have a global distribution.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C geographic distribution map

claim: Tumours that diverged early in the clade 1 lineage occur in Russia, Ukraine, China and India.
source: Tumours that diverged early in the clade 1 lineage occur in Russia, Ukraine, China and India, suggesting an Old World origin for this clade (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown in phylogenetic tree in Figure 1D

claim: Clade 1 has an Old World origin.
source: Tumours that diverged early in the clade 1 lineage occur in Russia, Ukraine, China and India, suggesting an Old World origin for this clade (Figure 1D).
evidence: Inferred from geographic distribution of early-diverging tumours

claim: Clade 1 tumours in Central and South America share a single common ancestor that probably existed no more than 511 years ago.
source: Clade 1 tumours in Central and South America share a single common ancestor that probably existed no more than 511 years ago, suggesting introduction of CTVT to the Americas with colonial contact; similarly, our data suggest a single introduction of CTVT to Australia after European arrival (maximum 116 years ago) (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 9, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculated from phylogenetic analysis and mutation rates

claim: CTVT was introduced to the Americas with colonial contact.
source: Clade 1 tumours in Central and South America share a single common ancestor that probably existed no more than 511 years ago, suggesting introduction of CTVT to the Americas with colonial contact; similarly, our data suggest a single introduction of CTVT to Australia after European arrival (maximum 116 years ago) (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 9, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Inferred from timing of common ancestor and historical context

claim: CTVT was introduced to Australia after European arrival (maximum 116 years ago).
source: Clade 1 tumours in Central and South America share a single common ancestor that probably existed no more than 511 years ago, suggesting introduction of CTVT to the Americas with colonial contact; similarly, our data suggest a single introduction of CTVT to Australia after European arrival (maximum 116 years ago) (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 9, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculated from phylogenetic analysis and mutation rates

claim: Clade 2 may have been transported between continents via trans-Atlantic and Indian Ocean trade routes.
source: The distribution pattern and timing of clade 2 suggest that this clade may have been transported between continents via trans-Atlantic and Indian Ocean trade routes (Figure 1C and 1D).
evidence: Inferred from geographic distribution and timing

claim: Clade 3 lineage was found in Central and South America and India.
source: The more recent clade 3 lineage was found in Central and South America and India, and the less frequent clades 4 and 5 occurred only in India and Nigeria respectively (Figure 1C and 1D).
evidence: Shown in geographic distribution map

claim: Clade 4 occurred only in India.
source: The more recent clade 3 lineage was found in Central and South America and India, and the less frequent clades 4 and 5 occurred only in India and Nigeria respectively (Figure 1C and 1D).
evidence: Shown in geographic distribution map

claim: Clade 5 occurred only in Nigeria.
source: The more recent clade 3 lineage was found in Central and South America and India, and the less frequent clades 4 and 5 occurred only in India and Nigeria respectively (Figure 1C and 1D).
evidence: Shown in geographic distribution map

claim: The extensive and recent global expansion detected in the CTVT lineage is consistent with signals of widespread admixture observed in worldwide populations of domestic dogs.
source: The extensive and recent global expansion detected in the CTVT lineage is consistent with signals of widespread admixture observed in worldwide populations of domestic dogs (Shannon et al., 2015), highlighting the extent to which canine companions accompanied human travellers on their global explorations.
evidence: Supported by citation to dog population genetics study

claim: Most somatic mutations in cancer are believed to be selectively neutral.
source: Most somatic mutations in cancer are believed to be selectively neutral, and there is little evidence in human cancers for negative selection operating to safeguard essential cellular processes (Stratton et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to cancer genomics literature

claim: There is little evidence in human cancers for negative selection operating to safeguard essential cellular processes.
source: Most somatic mutations in cancer are believed to be selectively neutral, and there is little evidence in human cancers for negative selection operating to safeguard essential cellular processes (Stratton et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to cancer genomics literature

claim: The variant allele fraction (VAF) of nonsense substitutions was significantly lower than VAF for other substitutions (p=0.00019).
source: Consistent with this prediction, the variant allele fraction (VAF) of nonsense substitutions and frameshift indels was significantly lower than VAF for other substitutions and indels (Figure 2A and B, p=0.00019 and p=3.03x10-05 respectively, two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: The variant allele fraction (VAF) of frameshift indels was significantly lower than VAF for other indels (p=3.03x10-05).
source: Consistent with this prediction, the variant allele fraction (VAF) of nonsense substitutions and frameshift indels was significantly lower than VAF for other substitutions and indels (Figure 2A and B, p=0.00019 and p=3.03x10-05 respectively, two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: dN/dS for somatic mtDNA mutations in CTVT showed significant deviation from neutrality for nonsense mutations (0.187, p=1.02x10-07).
source: Furthermore, dN/dS for somatic mtDNA mutations in CTVT showed significant deviation from neutrality both for nonsense (0.187, p=1.02x10-07) and missense (0.748, p=4.18x10-03) mutations (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by dN/dS analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: dN/dS for somatic mtDNA mutations in CTVT showed significant deviation from neutrality for missense mutations (0.748, p=4.18x10-03).
source: Furthermore, dN/dS for somatic mtDNA mutations in CTVT showed significant deviation from neutrality both for nonsense (0.187, p=1.02x10-07) and missense (0.748, p=4.18x10-03) mutations (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by dN/dS analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: Negative selection has operated to preserve mtDNA function in CTVT.
source: Together with evidence of reduced VAF for truncating mtDNA mutations in human cancers (Ju et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 2015), these findings provide evidence for the activity of negative selection operating to preserve mtDNA function in CTVT and indicate that, at least in some cancers, functional mtDNA contributes to driving cancer.
evidence: Supported by VAF and dN/dS analyses

claim: In at least some cancers, functional mtDNA contributes to driving cancer.
source: Together with evidence of reduced VAF for truncating mtDNA mutations in human cancers (Ju et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 2015), these findings provide evidence for the activity of negative selection operating to preserve mtDNA function in CTVT and indicate that, at least in some cancers, functional mtDNA contributes to driving cancer.
evidence: Inferred from evidence of negative selection in CTVT and human cancers

claim: MtDNA is usually assumed to be clonally inherited and recombinationally inert.
source: MtDNA is usually assumed to be clonally inherited and recombinationally inert.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: MtDNA recombination has been directly observed in various eukaryotes.
source: However, mtDNA recombination has been directly observed in various eukaryotes (Lunt and Hyman, 1997; Hoarau et al., 2002; Ladoukakis and Zouros, 2001; Gantenbein et al., 2005; Ujvari et al., 2007; Bergthorsson et al., 2003) and has been proposed as a mechanism for mtDNA repair (Thyagarajan et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: MtDNA recombination has been proposed as a mechanism for mtDNA repair.
source: However, mtDNA recombination has been directly observed in various eukaryotes (Lunt and Hyman, 1997; Hoarau et al., 2002; Ladoukakis and Zouros, 2001; Gantenbein et al., 2005; Ujvari et al., 2007; Bergthorsson et al., 2003) and has been proposed as a mechanism for mtDNA repair (Thyagarajan et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Recombination of maternal and paternal mtDNA haplotypes has been observed in rare cases of human biparental mtDNA inheritance.
source: Recombination of maternal and paternal mtDNA haplotypes has been observed in rare cases of human biparental mtDNA inheritance (Kraytsberg et al., 2004; Zsurka et al., 2005), and mtDNA recombination activity is present in human cell extracts (Thyagarajan et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: MtDNA recombination activity is present in human cell extracts.
source: Recombination of maternal and paternal mtDNA haplotypes has been observed in rare cases of human biparental mtDNA inheritance (Kraytsberg et al., 2004; Zsurka et al., 2005), and mtDNA recombination activity is present in human cell extracts (Thyagarajan et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: MtDNA recombination has not been previously detected in cancer.
source: However, mtDNA recombination has not, to our knowledge, been previously detected in cancer.
evidence: Statement of novelty based on literature review

claim: Recombination-detection algorithms 3seq and SiScan detected significant evidence for mtDNA recombination in CTVT clade 1.
source: Remarkably, these algorithms detected significant evidence for mtDNA recombination in CTVT clade 1, detecting recombination breakpoints at around MT:5430 and MT:16176.
evidence: Supported by computational recombination detection analysis

claim: Recombination breakpoints were detected at around MT:5430 and MT:16176 in CTVT clade 1.
source: Remarkably, these algorithms detected significant evidence for mtDNA recombination in CTVT clade 1, detecting recombination breakpoints at around MT:5430 and MT:16176.
evidence: Supported by computational recombination detection analysis

claim: Maximum likelihood phylogenetic trees constructed using segments MT:1–5429 and MT:5430–16176 derived from clade 1 mtDNA produced distinct topologies.
source: Maximum likelihood phylogenetic trees constructed using segments MT:1–5429 and MT:5430–16176 derived from clade 1 mtDNA produced distinct topologies (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A phylogenetic trees

claim: Recombination replaced MT:1–5429 in a clade 1 mtDNA haplotype that diverged from Central American clade 1 CTVTs and subsequently colonised areas of South and Central America (Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Paraguay).
source: Further inspection of clade 1 mtDNA haplotypes suggested that recombination replaced MT:1–5429 in a clade 1 mtDNA haplotype that diverged from Central American clade 1 CTVTs and that subsequently colonised areas of South and Central America (Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Paraguay) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis and geographic distribution

claim: 559T is a CTVT tumour derived from a male dog in Nicaragua.
source: This analysis identified 559T, a CTVT tumour derived from a male dog in Nicaragua (Figure 3C).
evidence: Sample information from study data

claim: 559T contains what appears to be a CTVT clade 1 mtDNA haplotype (CTVT_1B2b1_29) superimposed upon a dog mtDNA haplotype (A1d1a_1).
source: Further investigation of mtDNA in 559T revealed what appeared to be a CTVT clade 1 mtDNA haplotype (CTVT_1B2b1_29) superimposed upon a dog mtDNA haplotype (A1d1a_1), neither of which resembled the mtDNA haplotype found in normal tissues from this host dog, 559H (B1_1 haplotype).
evidence: Determined from sequence analysis

claim: The mtDNA haplotypes in 559T do not resemble the mtDNA haplotype found in normal tissues from host dog 559H (B1_1 haplotype).
source: Further investigation of mtDNA in 559T revealed what appeared to be a CTVT clade 1 mtDNA haplotype (CTVT_1B2b1_29) superimposed upon a dog mtDNA haplotype (A1d1a_1), neither of which resembled the mtDNA haplotype found in normal tissues from this host dog, 559H (B1_1 haplotype).
evidence: Determined from sequence analysis

claim: Phasing of mtDNA variants in 559T using long sequence reads indicated the presence of at least three distinct mtDNA haplotypes in this tumour.
source: Phasing of mtDNA variants in 559T using long sequence reads indicated the presence of at least three distinct mtDNA haplotypes in this tumour, each representing a recombination product apparently derived from mtDNA haplotypes CTVT_1B2b1_29 and A1d1a_1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by PacBio long-read sequencing data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Each of the three distinct mtDNA haplotypes in 559T represents a recombination product apparently derived from mtDNA haplotypes CTVT_1B2b1_29 and A1d1a_1.
source: Phasing of mtDNA variants in 559T using long sequence reads indicated the presence of at least three distinct mtDNA haplotypes in this tumour, each representing a recombination product apparently derived from mtDNA haplotypes CTVT_1B2b1_29 and A1d1a_1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Inferred from long-read sequencing data

claim: A tumour antecedent of 559T captured haplotype A1d1a_1 mtDNA from its host.
source: These data suggest that a tumour antecedent of 559T captured haplotype A1d1a_1 mtDNA from its host.
evidence: Inferred from presence of recombinant haplotypes

claim: Recombination was initiated between mtDNA haplotypes CTVT_1B2b1_29 and A1d1a_1 in 559T.
source: Recombination was initiated between mtDNA haplotypes CTVT_1B2b1_29 and A1d1a_1, and cells containing these recombination products were passed to host 559H.
evidence: Inferred from presence of recombinant haplotypes

claim: Cells containing recombination products were passed to host 559H.
source: Recombination was initiated between mtDNA haplotypes CTVT_1B2b1_29 and A1d1a_1, and cells containing these recombination products were passed to host 559H.
evidence: Inferred from presence of recombinant haplotypes in tumour

claim: It is possible that 559H received a mixture of both normal and CTVT cells from its CTVT donor animal, and mtDNA capture and recombination occurred within 559H.
source: Alternatively it is possible that 559H received a mixture of both normal and CTVT cells from its CTVT donor animal, and mtDNA capture and recombination occurred within 559H.
evidence: Alternative hypothesis proposed by authors

claim: The A1d1a_1 haplotype resembles the CTVT clade 3 donor haplotype.
source: It must also be mentioned that the A1d1a_1 haplotype resembles the CTVT clade 3 donor haplotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 4); thus we cannot exclude the possibility that the recombination that we observe in 559T involved horizontal transfer between clade 1 and clade 3 CTVT tumours that occurred within the same animal.
evidence: Observed from haplotype comparison in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: The recombination observed in 559T may have involved horizontal transfer between clade 1 and clade 3 CTVT tumours that occurred within the same animal.
source: It must also be mentioned that the A1d1a_1 haplotype resembles the CTVT clade 3 donor haplotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 4); thus we cannot exclude the possibility that the recombination that we observe in 559T involved horizontal transfer between clade 1 and clade 3 CTVT tumours that occurred within the same animal.
evidence: Alternative hypothesis proposed by authors

claim: Occasional mtDNA recombination activity occurs in CTVT cells.
source: Our analysis provides evidence for occasional mtDNA recombination activity in CTVT cells.
evidence: Supported by recombination detection in clade 1 and 559T

claim: A truncating nonsense mutation in COX3 was found in some 559T haplotypes.
source: Further analysis will determine if DNA damage signalling is involved, and it is interesting to observe that a truncating nonsense mutation in COX3 was found in some 559T haplotypes (Figure 3C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3C

claim: Evidence of negative selection demonstrates that maintenance of functional mtDNA is important for the biology of CTVT.
source: Evidence of negative selection demonstrates that maintenance of functional mtDNA is important for the biology of CTVT; and the observation of multiple mtDNA horizontal transfer events further supports the possibility that mtDNA capture from hosts is a positively selected adaptive mechanism (Rebbeck et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2015; Spees et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from selection analysis results

claim: Multiple mtDNA horizontal transfer events support the possibility that mtDNA capture from hosts is a positively selected adaptive mechanism.
source: Evidence of negative selection demonstrates that maintenance of functional mtDNA is important for the biology of CTVT; and the observation of multiple mtDNA horizontal transfer events further supports the possibility that mtDNA capture from hosts is a positively selected adaptive mechanism (Rebbeck et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2015; Spees et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from observation of five horizontal transfer events and supported by citations

claim: This study highlights the important role of functional mtDNA in cancer.
source: This study highlights the important role of functional mtDNA in cancer and reveals unexpected biological mechanisms that have operated in an ancient mammalian somatic cell lineage.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on study findings

claim: Unexpected biological mechanisms have operated in an ancient mammalian somatic cell lineage.
source: This study highlights the important role of functional mtDNA in cancer and reveals unexpected biological mechanisms that have operated in an ancient mammalian somatic cell lineage.
evidence: Summary conclusion referring to mtDNA recombination and horizontal transfer findings

claim: Whole genome sequencing libraries with insert size 100 to 400 base pairs were constructed.
source: Whole genome sequencing libraries with insert size 100 to 400 base pairs (bp) were constructed using standard methods according to manufacturer's instructions and sequenced with 75bp paired end reads on an Illumina HiSeq2000 instrument (Illumina, San Diego, CA) to an average whole genome depth of 0.3X; average mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) coverage was ~70X.
evidence: Directly stated in methods

claim: Sequencing was performed with 75bp paired end reads on an Illumina HiSeq2000 instrument.
source: Whole genome sequencing libraries with insert size 100 to 400 base pairs (bp) were constructed using standard methods according to manufacturer's instructions and sequenced with 75bp paired end reads on an Illumina HiSeq2000 instrument (Illumina, San Diego, CA) to an average whole genome depth of 0.3X; average mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) coverage was ~70X.
evidence: Directly stated in methods

claim: Reads were aligned with the CanFam3.1 dog reference genome using the BWA alignment tool.
source: Reads were aligned with the CanFam3.1 dog reference genome (Lindblad-Toh et al., 2005) (http://www.ensembl.org/Canis_familiaris/Info/Index) using the BWA alignment tool (Li and Durbin, 2009).
evidence: Directly stated in methods

claim: The ploidy used in mtDNA copy number calculations was 2 for both CTVT tumours and CTVT hosts.
source: The ploidy used in our calculations was 2 for both CTVT tumours and CTVT hosts (Murchison et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in methods with citation support

claim: Substitutions were called using CaVEMan (Cancer Variants through Expectation Maximisation).
source: Substitutions were called using CaVEMan (Cancer Variants through Expectation Maximisation), an in-house variant calling algorithm, as previously described (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012) (http://cancerit.github.io/CaVEMan/).
evidence: Directly stated in methods

claim: Phylogenetic trees were constructed using a maximum likelihood (ML) method implemented in PhyML 3.0.
source: Phylogenetic trees were constructed using a maximum likelihood (ML) method implemented in PhyML 3.0 (Guindon et al., 2010) using the General Time Reversible (GTR) + G + I nucleotide substitution model with transition/transversion (ts/tv) ratio, gamma distribution shape parameter and proportion of invariant sites estimated in PhyML for each dataset.
evidence: Directly stated in methods

claim: The General Time Reversible (GTR) + G + I nucleotide substitution model was used for phylogenetic tree construction.
source: Phylogenetic trees were constructed using a maximum likelihood (ML) method implemented in PhyML 3.0 (Guindon et al., 2010) using the General Time Reversible (GTR) + G + I nucleotide substitution model with transition/transversion (ts/tv) ratio, gamma distribution shape parameter and proportion of invariant sites estimated in PhyML for each dataset.
evidence: Directly stated in methods

claim: Bootstrap support values were obtained from 100 bootstrap replicates.
source: Bootstrap support values were obtained from 100 bootstrap replicates.
evidence: Directly stated in methods

claim: One homoplasmic somatic mtDNA mutation arises every ~1000 cell generations in human cancers.
source: A study of mtDNA mutations in human cancers estimated that one homoplasmic somatic mtDNA mutation arises every ~1000 cell generations in human cancers (Ju et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: CTVT cell generation times are 4 days for first stage tumours and >20 days for second stage tumours.
source: An experimental study estimated CTVT cell generation times to be 4 days for first stage tumours and >20 days for second stage tumours (Cohen and Steel, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous experimental study

claim: The RDP4 package was used to detect recombination events using a Bonferroni corrected p-value cutoff of 0.05.
source: The RDP4 package (Martin et al., 2015) was used to detect recombination events within the complete sample set (i.e. 449 CTVT tumours, 338 CTVT hosts and 252 additional dogs) using a Bonferroni corrected p-value cutoff of 0.05.
